A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same initialization-scale study. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices support comparison, including material relocated in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer and Emb-MLP experiments on synthetic tasks, GPT-2 training on PrOntoQA/TinyStories, and embedding and attention analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds initialization comparisons, language-embedding analyses, Layer Normalization ablations and learning-rate experiments.

M1.justification: The specified Gaussian initialization changes from variance d2^(-2γ), using the output dimension, in v1 Section 3.4 to d1^(-2γ), using the input dimension, in v2 Section 2.4. The core architectures, objectives and prediction procedures remain unchanged. This establishes a specification change, not whether implementations were changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic reasoning/memory mappings and PrOntoQA/TinyStories language tasks. The added experiments vary initialization, normalization and learning rate within retained coverage; they introduce no new dataset or input scenario.

E2.justification: The GPT-2 experiment adds γ=0.3 and γ=0.5 initialization comparators alongside γ=0.8, previously evaluated alone for language tasks (v2 Section 3.4, Figure 7A). These comparators already appeared in synthetic experiments. No external baseline algorithm is added.

E3.justification: v2 adds the relative-loss metric ΔL=(LTinyStories−LPrOntoQA)/LPrOntoQA and controlled GPT-2 initialization comparisons. New protocols include removing Layer Normalization with curves extending to 2,000 epochs and testing additional learning rates in Appendix G. Existing datasets, splits and principal training settings are retained; the revised initialization specification does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands checks of the proposed explanation: Section 3.4 tests initialization dependence in language training, Appendix C.5 examines language embeddings under larger initialization, Appendix F tests whether normalization is necessary, and Appendix G tests learning-rate sensitivity. Existing Emb-MLP embedding analyses also receive revised heatmaps.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run aggregates, confidence intervals or significance tests for these experiments. The additional plots introduce no uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: New results show larger relative language-loss gaps with increasing γ, reasoning bias without Layer Normalization and across tested learning rates, and instability at learning rate 0.001. Emb-MLP similarities change in v1 Figure 3/v2 Figure 4 and Appendix Figure 10, including a less ordered late-stage memory-anchor pattern. The language cosine averages 0.123 and 0.531 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 revises Lemma 2's gradient expression, and B.2 adds missing support indicators to key/noise-label distributions. Appendix E.3 revises the existing attention construction; former Theorem 4 remains as a derivation, while Theorem 3 becomes Lemma 5. Section 3.4 defines ΔL. The principal propositions and theoretical scope are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: smaller initialization favors reasoning, and label distributions shape embedding differentiation and attention behavior. New experiments support these existing contributions without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Appendix C.5 newly interprets near-orthogonal language embeddings under larger initialization as neglecting token associations. Appendix G adds a concrete applicability boundary: training becomes unstable at learning rate 0.001. The central label-distribution explanation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 specifies checkpoints previously described only generally, including step 5,000 for language embeddings and epoch 200 for first-attention analysis. Appendix A.2 and the new appendices document the added initialization and ablation settings. Existing model dimensions, sample counts, batch size and optimizer details are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to GPT-4, DeepSeek-V3, Breiman's generalization discussion, Zhang et al. on rethinking generalization, and Xu et al.'s condensation overview. These provide limited additional context; positioning around initialization, anchor functions and low-rank versus condensed representations remains stable.

P1.justification: Most prose is retained with limited editing and added explanatory headings. Related Works moves from Section 2 to Section 4, and the synthetic-task example moves from Appendix A.1 into the main presentation. Acknowledgements and an Impact Statement are added.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint is extensively reformatted into an ICML layout with a two-column main text. The task schematic moves into the main paper, the language figure gains a loss-gap panel, embedding heatmaps are redrawn and rescaled, and new figures present language-embedding and robustness analyses.

improvement.justification: The controlled GPT-2 comparisons address v1's missing initialization controls for language tasks, while the normalization and learning-rate tests strengthen robustness evidence and identify an instability boundary. Probability-support corrections also improve precision. These provide a limited net gain, although v2's revised initialization convention remains inconsistent with the output-dimension scaling retained in Appendix B.4.
